# Nigeria — Builder Mode

## Builder-Mode Scope

- This file derives strictly from `evidence.md`, `signals.md`, `trust-dimensions.md`, `metadata.md`, and `profile.md` for Nigeria.
- It describes builder-facing operational interaction only across continuity, interoperability, administration, digital services, payments, telecommunications, electricity, transportation, aviation, maritime administration, emergency coordination, cyber coordination, research networking, regional interconnection, dependency structure, and bounded observability.
- No rankings, scores, trust levels, readiness levels, certifications, deployment meanings, deployment guidance, or Atlas surface assignments exist in this file.
- No geopolitical interpretation, West Africa leadership interpretation, Africa-leadership interpretation, regional-power interpretation, oil-and-gas interpretation, population-scale interpretation, economic-power interpretation, fintech interpretation, mobile-money interpretation, security/conflict interpretation, gateway-to-Africa interpretation, or strategic-geography interpretation exists in this file.
- All statements remain evidence-bound, renderer-safe, and bounded by incomplete public observability.

## Administrative Interaction Environment

- The administrative interaction environment presents as an Abuja-centered coordination structure linked to federal ministries, departments, agencies, service portals, regulators, and supervised institutions rather than a single consolidated administrative stack.
- Abuja-centered coordination is visible through the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation and wider federal administrative surfaces, while execution remains distributed across a thirty-six-state environment and multiple sectoral institutions rather than staying confined to one administrative site.
- OSGF interaction, ministry-department-agency interaction, regulator-service interaction, and federal-service interaction are visible as overlapping administrative continuity layers rather than a single outward-facing service structure.
- State-level interaction is visible because federal coordination coexists with territorially distributed continuity rather than a capital-only administrative model.
- Public-service interaction remains capital-centered in coordination terms but territorially distributed in execution and service access.
- From a builder-facing perspective, continuity appears here through centralized coordination with distributed execution across overlapping administrative and public-service systems.

## Identity & Digital-Service Interaction Environment

- The identity and digital-service interaction environment appears through National Identity Management Commission interaction, National Identification Number interaction, identity-registration interaction, identity-service interaction, identity-data update interaction, and federal service-access interaction rather than disconnected access channels.
- NIMC makes national identity-administration interaction visible through enrolment, NIN issuance, and identity-record continuity rather than portal-only credential behavior.
- NIN workflows make identity-registration interaction visible through recurring national identity handling rather than one-time document issuance.
- Federal service-access surfaces make digital public-service interaction visible through online access layers linked to identity administration rather than isolated portal exposure.
- The coexistence of NIMC and federal service-access workflows makes identity-service interaction and public-service continuity visible inside the same broader administrative environment rather than as unrelated systems.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as layered identity, registration, and digital public-service interaction under bounded observability and without surveillance inference or unsupported claims about hidden identity capability.

## Payment & Financial Interaction Environment

- The payment and financial interaction environment appears through Central Bank of Nigeria interaction, National Payments System interaction, Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System interaction, RTGS and S4 interaction, NIBSS Instant Payment interaction, Nigeria Central Switch interaction, licensed-provider interaction, and settlement interoperability rather than fragmented institution-specific transfer behavior.
- CBN makes central-bank-administered payment interaction visible through coordination, supervision, rules, settlement, and participant oversight rather than diffuse bilateral transfer arrangements.
- National Payments System interaction is visible through multiple participant classes and multiple payment rails rather than a single settlement path.
- RTGS and S4 make large-value settlement interaction visible inside the wider payment environment rather than a payment structure limited to retail or deferred flows.
- NIBSS makes interbank interoperability interaction visible, while NIBSS Instant Payment makes instant-payment interaction visible inside the wider settlement environment rather than isolated bank-by-bank transfer channels.
- The Nigeria Central Switch makes switching interaction and interconnectivity interaction visible rather than detached payment-routing silos.
- Licensed-provider surfaces make banking and provider interaction visible across switching, processing, card-scheme, and payment-service layers rather than a closed bank-only arrangement.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as payment-settlement interoperability interaction through layered central-bank coordination, interbank settlement, switching, and provider participation, kept strictly operational and without fintech, mobile-money, or economic-power narratives.

## Telecommunications & Connectivity Interaction Environment

- The telecommunications and connectivity interaction environment appears through Nigerian Communications Commission interaction, `.ng` interaction, Nigeria Internet Registration Association interaction, Internet Exchange Point of Nigeria interaction, naming-governance interaction, and internet-exchange interaction rather than a purely operator-defined communications environment.
- NCC makes communications-regulatory interaction visible through sector oversight rather than commercial operator activity alone.
- NiRA and `.ng` administration make naming-governance interaction visible through a formal country-domain structure rather than unmanaged namespace activity.
- IXPN makes internet-exchange interaction and interconnection interaction visible rather than traffic exchange remaining implicit inside private operator relationships alone.
- The wider connectivity environment presents as regulated, administratively structured, and partially visible, while deeper private backbone, full carrier interconnection, enterprise-topology, and commercial operator details remain only partly visible.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as telecom-domain-exchange interaction under bounded observability and without innovation-hub, startup-ecosystem, or digital-leadership narratives.

## Electricity & Energy Interaction Environment

- The electricity and energy interaction environment appears through Transmission Company of Nigeria interaction, Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission interaction, Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc interaction, transmission interaction, system-operation interaction, and electricity coordination rather than a single undifferentiated electricity system.
- TCN makes transmission interaction and system-operation interaction visible through a named transmission and system-operations layer rather than electricity visibility confined to distribution edges.
- Public differentiation between TCN and distribution companies makes transmission-distribution separation visible rather than one undifferentiated electricity structure.
- NERC makes electricity-regulatory interaction visible, while NBET makes electricity-pool-administration interaction visible inside the wider electricity environment.
- The coexistence of TCN, NERC, and NBET makes electricity-regulator-transmission interaction visible across overlapping transmission, regulation, and pool-administration layers rather than a single governance surface.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as electricity-regulator-transmission interaction and electricity coordination kept strictly operational and without oil-and-gas, resource, or strategic-energy narratives.

## Transportation Interaction Environment

- The transportation interaction environment appears through Federal Ministry of Transportation interaction, Federal Ministry of Works interaction, Federal Roads Maintenance Agency interaction, Nigerian Railway Corporation interaction, road interaction, rail interaction, and multimodal interaction rather than a single-mode terrestrial transport structure.
- The Federal Ministry of Transportation makes national transport-coordination interaction visible across rail, road transport, mass transit, maritime services, and transport planning rather than infrastructure visibility without a coordinating layer.
- The Federal Ministry of Works and FERMA make federal-road interaction and road-maintenance interaction visible rather than static road ownership visibility alone.
- NRC makes rail interaction visible through passenger, excursion, freight, and route-service surfaces rather than historical rail presence alone.
- Federal transport coordination, federal works continuity, road maintenance, and rail operations together make multimodal interaction and recurring road-rail interaction visible rather than isolated modal systems.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as distributed road continuity, rail continuity, and multimodal interaction kept strictly operational and without gateway, corridor, or logistics-dominance narratives.

## Aviation Interaction Environment

- The aviation interaction environment appears through Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority interaction, Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria interaction, Nigerian Airspace Management Agency interaction, airport-management interaction, air-navigation interaction, and distributed airport continuity rather than airport activity in isolation.
- NCAA makes aviation-oversight interaction and economic-regulation interaction visible rather than airport handling alone.
- FAAN makes airport-management interaction visible through a multi-airport operating environment rather than airport-by-airport isolated administration.
- NAMA makes air-navigation interaction and airspace-management interaction visible rather than oversight without a named operational navigation layer.
- Abuja, Lagos, Kano, Port Harcourt, and Enugu make distributed airport continuity visible rather than aviation continuity being confined to one node.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as regulator-operator-navigation interaction and distributed airport continuity without aviation-hub rhetoric or gateway framing.

## Maritime & Port Interaction Environment

- The maritime and port interaction environment appears through Nigerian Ports Authority interaction, Lagos Port Complex interaction, Tin Can Island interaction, Onne interaction, National Inland Waterways Authority interaction, Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency interaction, and maritime administration interaction rather than a single national port surface.
- NPA makes port-governance interaction and port-operations interaction visible through a formal public port-administration layer rather than fragmented port-by-port governance.
- Lagos Port Complex, Tin Can Island, and Onne make multi-port interaction visible inside the wider port environment rather than maritime continuity centered on one site alone.
- NIWA makes inland-waterway interaction visible rather than maritime continuity being limited to seaports.
- NIMASA makes maritime-safety interaction and shipping-regulation interaction visible rather than port administration being the whole maritime model.
- NPA, NIWA, and NIMASA together make maritime administration interaction visible through overlapping port, inland-waterway, and maritime-regulatory layers rather than one isolated maritime function.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as maritime-support interaction and multi-port continuity without gateway-to-Africa, strategic-port, trade-dominance, or oil-export narratives.

## Disaster-Response & Emergency Coordination Interaction Environment

- The disaster-response and emergency coordination interaction environment appears through National Emergency Management Agency interaction rather than ad hoc emergency assembly.
- NEMA makes preparedness interaction, emergency-coordination interaction, response-coordination interaction, warning interaction, and assessment interaction visible through standing public and coordination surfaces rather than event-only crisis administration.
- Public incident updates, early-warning activity, and multi-agency response visibility make recurring preparedness and response interaction visible rather than isolated emergency notices.
- Territorial-office visibility makes distributed territorial emergency continuity visible rather than a capital-confined emergency structure.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as a nationally coordinated and territorially distributed emergency-interaction layer kept strictly operational and without security/conflict framing or performance scoring.

## Cybersecurity & Data Interaction Environment

- The cybersecurity and data interaction environment appears through National Information Technology Development Agency interaction, Nigeria Computer Emergency Response Team interaction, National Cybersecurity Coordination Centre interaction where evidenced, Nigeria Data Protection Commission interaction, cyber-response coordination, and data-governance interaction rather than a single cyber or data platform.
- NITDA makes IT-governance interaction visible through planning, coordination, monitoring, and regulation continuity rather than isolated policy publication.
- ngCERT makes cyber-response interaction and public incident-contact interaction visible rather than organization-by-organization escalation alone.
- NCCC makes federal cybersecurity-coordination interaction visible where evidenced rather than cyber-governance being limited to one public institution.
- NDPC makes data-governance interaction and public compliance-interface interaction visible rather than privacy administration remaining fully diffuse.
- NITDA, ngCERT, NCCC where evidenced, and NDPC together make cyber-data-governance interaction visible across overlapping IT-governance, cyber-response, coordination, and data-protection layers.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as a public-sector cyber-response and data-governance interaction layer under bounded observability and does not support hidden cyber-capability inference.

## Research & Education Network Interaction Environment

- The research and education network interaction environment appears through Nigerian Research and Education Network interaction, academic-network interaction, institutional-connectivity interaction, eduroam interaction where evidenced, and research-service interaction rather than reliance on commercial connectivity alone.
- NgREN makes research-network interaction visible as a named national academic-network layer rather than an informal educational overlay.
- Institutional connectivity makes member-serving academic interconnection visible rather than isolated campus networking.
- eduroam visibility and externally linked administrative references make federated access interaction visible where evidenced rather than a domestic-only academic perimeter.
- Connectivity infrastructure, computing support, capacity-building, and related services make research-service interaction visible inside the wider research-network environment rather than standalone network provision.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as research-network-connectivity interaction and research-network-supported continuity kept operational only and without innovation-state rhetoric.

## Regional & International Interconnection Interaction Environment

- The regional and international interconnection interaction environment appears through `.ng` external interaction, IXPN interconnection, NgREN external relationships, AfriNIC and ICANN interaction where evidenced, aviation interfaces, maritime interfaces, and standards interaction where evidenced rather than one dominant outward-facing interface.
- `.ng` administration and IXPN make external naming-governance interaction and interconnection interaction visible inside the wider connectivity environment.
- NgREN makes externally linked research-network interaction visible through administrative relationships and service continuity where evidenced rather than a purely domestic academic perimeter.
- AfriNIC and ICANN references make external administrative interaction visible where evidenced rather than unsupported regional or geopolitical interpretation.
- Aviation interfaces are visible through a multi-airport international layer, while maritime interfaces are visible through a multi-port environment rather than single-node external access.
- Maritime standards interaction is visible where evidenced through NIMASA's convention-linked mandate surfaces rather than unsupported strategic or geopolitical narratives.
- In the payment domain, public visibility remains stronger for national interoperability and settlement interaction than for specifically named regional payment-scheme interaction.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as layered regional and international interconnection without geopolitical framing, West Africa leadership narratives, regional-power narratives, or gateway narratives.

## Distributed Territorial Continuity Interaction Environment

- The distributed territorial continuity interaction environment appears as Abuja-centered federal coordination with Lagos-linked operational reinforcement and distributed multi-node territorial continuity rather than a single-node national operating model.
- Abuja-centered coordination is visible through federal administrative, regulatory, electricity, aviation, and service-access surfaces rather than a purely symbolic capital role.
- Lagos-linked reinforcement is visible through port administration, Lagos Port Complex, Tin Can Island, Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos-linked rail activity, and exchange infrastructure rather than a Lagos-only national model.
- Multi-state continuity is visible through the thirty-six-state environment and distributed federal-sector interfaces rather than one-city administrative relevance.
- Multi-port continuity is visible through Lagos, Tin Can, Rivers, Onne, Calabar, Delta, and related port-administration surfaces rather than one-port concentration.
- Multi-airport continuity is visible through Abuja, Lagos, Kano, Port Harcourt, and Enugu rather than aviation continuity being confined to one airport.
- Distributed road continuity, rail continuity, electricity continuity, and service continuity make territorial continuity visible across more than one operating zone rather than service continuity stopping at Abuja or Lagos.
- Nigeria is not Abuja-only, not Lagos-only, not oil-region-defined, and not population-defined in this builder-facing characterization.
- From a builder-facing perspective, this environment presents as distributed multi-node territorial continuity operating through federal coordination, Lagos-linked reinforcement, and territorially distributed infrastructure interaction.

## Cross-System Interaction Environment

- The strongest recurring interaction pattern is centralized coordination with distributed execution across federal administration, identity services, payment rails, communications governance, electricity coordination, transport administration, aviation oversight, port administration, emergency coordination, cyber coordination, and research-network functions rather than isolated sector operation.
- A second recurring pattern is continuity-through-overlapping systems, visible across administrative, identity, payment, telecommunications, electricity, transportation, aviation, maritime, emergency, cyber/data, and research-network layers rather than detached infrastructures.
- A third recurring pattern is interoperability as continuity, visible through identity-service interaction, interbank settlement and switching, naming-governance and exchange interaction, electricity regulation and transmission interaction, and research-network connectivity with external administrative interfaces.
- A fourth recurring pattern is identity-service interaction, because NIMC, NIN workflows, and federal service-access surfaces operate inside the same wider continuity environment rather than as unrelated systems.
- A fifth recurring pattern is payment-settlement interaction, because CBN, RTGS, S4, NIBSS, NIBSS Instant Payment, the Nigeria Central Switch, and licensed-provider structures form a layered settlement and interoperability environment rather than a single transaction pathway.
- A sixth recurring pattern is telecom-domain-exchange interaction, because NCC, NiRA, `.ng` administration, and IXPN operate as adjacent regulatory, naming, and interconnection layers within the same communications environment.
- A seventh recurring pattern is electricity-regulator-transmission interaction, because TCN, NERC, and NBET operate as overlapping transmission, regulatory, and pool-administration layers rather than one isolated electricity function.
- An eighth recurring pattern is road-rail-port-airport interaction, because transport coordination, road maintenance, rail operations, airport administration, and port administration reinforce the same wider territorial continuity environment.
- A ninth recurring pattern is cyber-data-governance interaction, because NITDA, ngCERT, NCCC where evidenced, and NDPC operate as overlapping IT-governance, cyber-response, cybersecurity-coordination, and data-protection layers.
- A tenth recurring pattern is research-network-connectivity interaction, because NgREN connectivity, eduroam continuity where evidenced, computing support, and external administrative relationships operate as part of the wider connectivity environment rather than as a disconnected academic enclave.
- From a builder-facing perspective, Nigeria presents as an Abuja-centered federal coordination environment with Lagos-linked reinforcement, distributed territorial continuity, payment-settlement interoperability, telecom-domain-exchange continuity, electricity coordination, maritime support, research-network support, regional interconnection, and bounded observability.

## Operational Visibility & Dependency Environment

- The operational environment is bounded by incomplete telecom visibility, incomplete private-network visibility, incomplete cyber-operational visibility, incomplete logistics visibility, incomplete electricity-market visibility, and incomplete commercial-topology visibility.
- Public visibility is stronger for federal administration, identity administration, digital-service access, payment rails, communications regulation, naming governance, exchange presence, electricity coordination, transport administration, aviation administration, port administration, emergency coordination, cyber coordination, data governance, and research-network structures than for deeper private operator topology.
- Visible continuity dependencies remain present on OSGF and federal service surfaces for federal administrative coordination, NIMC for identity continuity, CBN and the National Payments System for payment and settlement continuity, NIBSS for interbank interoperability, NCC for communications regulation, NiRA for `.ng` naming governance, IXPN for visible exchange continuity, TCN for transmission and system-operation continuity, NERC and NBET for electricity-sector coordination continuity, the Federal Ministry of Transportation, Federal Ministry of Works, FERMA, and NRC for transport continuity, NCAA, FAAN, and NAMA for aviation continuity, NPA, NIWA, and NIMASA for maritime continuity, NEMA for emergency coordination, NITDA, ngCERT, NCCC where evidenced, and NDPC for cyber and data-governance continuity, and NgREN for research-network continuity.
- Commercial backbone routes, detailed bank-to-bank dependencies beyond published rails, private telecom peering, terminal operating arrangements, private freight routing, inland warehousing, airport backend systems, and deeper cyber-operational tooling remain only partly visible in the upstream layers.
- Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
- Hidden-capability inference is prohibited.
- From a builder-facing perspective, Nigeria appears continuity-linked and partially visible, with stronger public observability for administrative and coordination layers than for full private and commercial operating detail.

## Builder-Oriented Structural Characterization

- Nigeria is characterized here as an Abuja-centered federal coordination environment with Lagos-linked operational reinforcement and distributed multi-node territorial continuity.
- It presents as a payment-settlement interoperability environment reinforced by central-bank coordination, interbank settlement, switching continuity, and licensed-provider interaction rather than isolated transaction pathways.
- It presents as a telecom-domain-exchange continuity environment with communications regulation, naming-governance continuity, and visible exchange interaction rather than an operator-only connectivity model.
- It presents as an electricity coordination environment in which transmission, system operation, regulation, and pool administration interact rather than appearing as detached electricity functions.
- It presents as a maritime-support continuity environment, a research-network-supported continuity environment, a regional interconnection environment, and a bounded-observability environment where publicly evidenced.
- Administrative, identity, payment, telecommunications, electricity, transportation, aviation, maritime, emergency, cyber/data, and research-network systems interact in layered form rather than as detached infrastructures.
- Centralized coordination with distributed execution is the dominant recurring structural pattern.
- Interoperability as continuity and continuity-through-overlapping systems are the second dominant recurring structural patterns.
- No ranking, scoring, recommendation, or geopolitical interpretation is implied by this characterization.
- Overall, the builder-facing characterization is that of an Abuja-centered federal coordination environment with Lagos-linked reinforcement, distributed territorial continuity, payment-settlement interoperability, telecom-domain-exchange continuity, electricity coordination, maritime support, research-network support, regional interconnection, and bounded observability.

## Structural Constraints & Interpretation Limits

- This file remains bounded to structural characteristics documented in `evidence.md`, `signals.md`, `trust-dimensions.md`, `metadata.md`, and `profile.md`.
- Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
- Hidden-capability inference is prohibited.
- No trust score, readiness level, certification meaning, or Atlas surface assignment is implied.
- No deployment meaning, deployment guidance, approval, or avoidance recommendation is implied.
- No interpretation as geopolitical power, West Africa leader, Africa leader, regional power, oil economy, population scale, economic power, fintech environment, mobile-money environment, cultural influence environment, security/conflict environment, or gateway environment is implied.
- Bounded observability remains part of the canonical record across telecom, private-network, cyber-operational, logistics, electricity-market, and commercial-topology layers.

# Nigeria — Profile

## Profile Scope

- This file derives strictly from `evidence.md`, `signals.md`, `trust-dimensions.md`, and `metadata.md` for Nigeria.
- This profile is evidence-bound and descriptive only.
- No rankings, trust scores, readiness levels, certifications, deployment meanings, or Atlas surface assignments are made in this file.
- No geopolitical interpretation, West Africa leadership interpretation, Africa-leadership interpretation, regional-power interpretation, oil-and-gas interpretation, population-scale interpretation, economic-power interpretation, fintech interpretation, mobile-money interpretation, security/conflict interpretation, gateway-to-Africa interpretation, or strategic-geography interpretation is implied.
- All profile statements remain renderer-safe and bounded by incomplete public observability.

## Jurisdiction Overview

- Nigeria presents as an Abuja-centered federal coordination environment with distributed state continuity and multi-node territorial continuity rather than a single-node national operating model.
- The visible operational environment is reinforced by payment-settlement interoperability, telecom-domain-exchange continuity, electricity coordination, maritime-support continuity, research-network-supported continuity, regional interconnection, and bounded observability.
- Public continuity is visible through overlapping administrative, identity, payment, telecommunications, electricity, transportation, aviation, maritime, emergency, cyber/data, and research-network layers rather than through one consolidated institutional stack.
- Lagos appears as an important operational reinforcement layer inside the wider federal and territorial environment, but the profile does not normalize Nigeria as Lagos-only any more than it normalizes it as Abuja-only.
- This overview remains strictly operational and does not adopt population-size, oil-resource, economic-power, or regional-leadership framing.

## Administrative Environment

- Nigeria presents as an Abuja-centered administrative environment whose visible continuity depends on federal ministries, departments, agencies, service portals, and regulator-operator relationships rather than on a single consolidated public-service stack.
- Administrative coordination is visibly concentrated through Abuja-facing federal institutions including the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation and wider federal service surfaces, while execution remains distributed across a thirty-six-state environment and multiple sectoral institutions.
- OSGF continuity, federal service access surfaces, and publicly visible supervised agencies indicate recurring federal coordination continuity rather than capital-only symbolic presence.
- The resulting administrative environment is one of centralized coordination with distributed execution, federal administrative continuity, state-level continuity, and distributed public-service operation.

## Identity & Digital-Service Environment

- The identity and digital-service environment is structured around National Identity Management Commission continuity, National Identification Number continuity, identity-registration continuity, identity-data update continuity, and federal service-portal continuity as interacting layers.
- NIMC provides the visible national identity-administration environment for enrolment, NIN issuance, and identity-record continuity.
- The resulting profile is one of identity-service continuity and digital-service continuity while remaining bounded against surveillance inference.

## Payment & Financial Environment

- The payment and financial environment is one of payment-settlement interoperability structured around Central Bank of Nigeria continuity, National Payments System continuity, Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System continuity, RTGS and S4 continuity, NIBSS Instant Payment continuity, Nigeria Central Switch continuity, and licensed-provider interaction.
- CBN provides visible central-bank payment coordination continuity through payment-system supervision, settlement administration, rules, and participant oversight.
- RTGS and S4 provide large-value settlement continuity within the wider payment environment.
- NIBSS provides interbank interoperability continuity, while NIBSS Instant Payment provides visible instant-payment continuity.
- The Nigeria Central Switch indicates switching continuity and interconnectivity continuity.
- The resulting profile is one of central-bank-coordinated settlement continuity, interbank interoperability continuity, and layered payment interaction kept strictly operational and without fintech, mobile-money, or economic-power narratives.

## Telecommunications & Connectivity Environment

- The telecommunications and connectivity environment is one of telecom-domain-exchange continuity structured around Nigerian Communications Commission continuity, `.ng` continuity, Nigeria Internet Registration Association continuity, Internet Exchange Point of Nigeria continuity, naming governance, and exchange visibility.
- NCC provides visible communications-regulatory continuity.
- NiRA and `.ng` administration provide country-domain governance continuity through a formal registry environment.
- IXPN provides visible internet-exchange continuity and recurring exchange activity.
- The resulting profile is one of telecommunications continuity and telecom-domain-exchange continuity with bounded visibility into private backbone routes and deeper commercial topology.

## Electricity & Energy Environment

- The electricity and energy environment is one of electricity coordination structured around Transmission Company of Nigeria continuity, Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission continuity, Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc continuity, transmission continuity, system-operation continuity, and pool-administration interaction.
- TCN provides the visible transmission and system-operations environment.
- NERC provides standing electricity-regulatory continuity, while NBET provides electricity-pool administration continuity.
- The resulting profile is one of transmission continuity, system-operation continuity, and electricity coordination kept strictly operational.

## Transportation Environment

- The transportation environment is coordinated through Federal Ministry of Transportation continuity, Federal Ministry of Works continuity, Federal Roads Maintenance Agency continuity, Nigerian Railway Corporation continuity, road continuity, rail continuity, and multimodal interaction.
- The resulting profile is one of distributed road continuity, rail continuity, and multimodal transport interaction kept strictly operational.

## Aviation Environment

- The aviation environment is coordinated through Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority continuity, Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria continuity, and Nigerian Airspace Management Agency continuity.
- The visibility of Abuja, Lagos, Kano, Port Harcourt, and Enugu airport nodes indicates distributed airport continuity.
- The resulting profile is one of regulator-operator-navigation continuity and distributed airport continuity without aviation-hub rhetoric.

## Maritime & Port Environment

- The maritime and port environment is one of maritime-support continuity structured around Nigerian Ports Authority continuity, Lagos Port Complex continuity, Tin Can Island Port Complex continuity, Onne Port Complex continuity, National Inland Waterways Authority continuity, and Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency continuity.
- The resulting profile is one of maritime administration continuity and maritime-support continuity kept strictly operational.

## Disaster-Response & Emergency Coordination Environment

- The disaster-response and emergency coordination environment is defined by National Emergency Management Agency continuity as the clearest visible national disaster-management and coordination layer.
- Territorial-office visibility indicates distributed emergency continuity rather than a capital-only emergency structure.

## Cybersecurity & Data Environment

- The cybersecurity and data environment is structured around National Information Technology Development Agency continuity, Nigeria Computer Emergency Response Team continuity, National Cybersecurity Coordination Centre continuity where evidenced, and Nigeria Data Protection Commission continuity.
- The resulting profile is one of cyber-response coordination and data-governance continuity while remaining bounded against hidden cyber-capability inference.

## Research & Education Network Environment

- The research and education network environment is one of research-network-supported continuity structured around Nigerian Research and Education Network continuity, academic-network continuity, institutional connectivity, eduroam continuity where evidenced, and research-service continuity.
- The resulting profile is one of research-network-supported continuity and institutional academic interconnection kept strictly operational.

## Regional & International Interconnection Environment

- The regional and international interconnection environment is layered across `.ng` continuity, IXPN interconnection, NgREN external interfaces, AfriNIC and ICANN administrative relationships where evidenced, aviation interfaces, maritime interfaces, and standards interaction.
- The resulting profile is one of layered regional and international interconnection kept strictly operational and without geopolitical, West Africa leadership, regional-power, gateway, or strategic-geography narratives.

## Distributed Territorial Continuity Environment

- Nigeria presents as an Abuja-centered but distributed territorial continuity environment rather than a single-node administrative system.
- Lagos provides visible operational reinforcement through port administration, Lagos Port Complex, Tin Can Island, Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos-linked rail activity, and exchange infrastructure.
- Multi-port continuity is visible through Lagos, Tin Can, Rivers, Onne, Calabar, Delta, and related port-administration surfaces.
- Multi-airport continuity is visible through Abuja, Lagos, Kano, Port Harcourt, and Enugu.
- Nigeria is not characterized here as Abuja-only, Lagos-only, oil-region-defined, or population-defined.

## Cross-System Operational Profile

- The strongest recurring pattern is centralized coordination with distributed execution across all sectors.
- A second recurring pattern is continuity-through-overlapping systems.
- A third recurring pattern is interoperability as continuity.
- Taken together, Nigeria presents as an Abuja-centered federal coordination environment with distributed territorial continuity, payment-settlement interoperability, telecom-domain-exchange continuity, electricity coordination, maritime support, research-network support, regional interconnection, and bounded observability.

## Observability Profile

- Bounded observability is a standing feature of the Nigeria profile.
- Incomplete telecom, private-network, cyber-operational, logistics, electricity-market, and commercial-topology visibility remain present.
- Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Hidden-capability inference is prohibited.

# Nigeria — Signals

## Signal Scope

- This file derives strictly from `evidence.md` for Nigeria and does not introduce new infrastructure claims.
- No rankings, trust scores, readiness scores, certifications, or Atlas surface assignments are used in this file.
- No geopolitical, West Africa leadership, Africa-leadership, regional-power, oil-and-gas, population-scale, economic-power, fintech, mobile-money, gateway-to-Africa, or strategic-geography interpretation is intended or supported.

## Administrative Continuity Signals

- The evidence indicates a signal of Abuja-centered federal coordination operating through federal offices, ministries, departments, agencies, and service portals rather than through a single consolidated public-service stack.
- The coexistence of the federal capital role, OSGF coordination, and publicly visible supervised agencies indicates a signal of recurring federal administrative continuity rather than capital-only symbolic presence.
- The coexistence of Abuja-centered federal coordination with a thirty-six-state environment indicates a signal of distributed state and sectoral continuity.
- The overall administrative pattern indicates centralized coordination with distributed execution.

## Identity & Digital-Service Signals

- NIMC indicates a signal of formal identity-administration continuity anchored to a national identification layer rather than isolated document issuance.
- The NIN framework indicates a signal of recurring national identity-registration continuity.
- The federal services portal indicates a signal of digital public-service access continuity.
- The coexistence of national identity administration with federal online service access indicates a signal of identity-service interaction and digital-physical service continuity.

## Payment & Financial Continuity Signals

- CBN indicates a signal of central-bank-administered payment coordination continuity through a visible national payments-system layer.
- RTGS and S4 indicate a signal of large-value settlement continuity.
- NIBSS indicates a signal of interbank interoperability continuity.
- NIBSS Instant Payment indicates a signal of instant-payment continuity inside the wider settlement environment.
- The Nigeria Central Switch indicates a signal of switching continuity and public interconnectivity continuity.
- CBN licensing surfaces indicate a signal of recurring licensed-provider interaction across card schemes, switching and processing, mobile-money operators, and payment solution providers.
- The combined evidence supports normalization of Nigeria as a payment-settlement interoperability environment.

## Telecommunications & Connectivity Signals

- NCC indicates a signal of regulatory continuity across the communications sector.
- NiRA indicates a signal of `.ng` naming-governance continuity through a formal country-domain administration layer.
- IXPN indicates a signal of visible internet-exchange continuity.
- The coexistence of communications regulation, `.ng` administration, and exchange infrastructure indicates a signal of telecommunications-continuity through overlapping regulatory, naming, and interconnection layers.

## Electricity & Energy Continuity Signals

- TCN indicates a signal of transmission continuity through a visible transmission and system-operations layer.
- NERC indicates a signal of electricity-regulatory continuity.
- NBET indicates a signal of electricity-pool administration continuity.
- The coexistence of TCN, NERC, and NBET indicates a signal of recurring electricity-sector coordination.

## Transportation Continuity Signals

- The Federal Ministry of Transportation indicates a signal of national transport-coordination continuity.
- FERMA indicates a signal of federal-road maintenance continuity.
- NRC indicates a signal of rail continuity through ongoing passenger, excursion, and freight surfaces.
- The coexistence of federal transport coordination, FERMA road maintenance, and NRC rail operations indicates a signal of road-rail interaction and layered transport continuity.

## Aviation Continuity Signals

- NCAA indicates a signal of aviation-oversight continuity.
- FAAN indicates a signal of airport-management continuity through a formal multi-airport operating layer.
- The visibility of Abuja, Lagos, Kano, Port Harcourt, and Enugu airport nodes indicates a signal of distributed multi-airport continuity.
- NAMA indicates a signal of airspace-management continuity.

## Maritime & Port Continuity Signals

- NPA indicates a signal of port-administration continuity through a formal federal port-governance and operations layer.
- Public identification of Lagos Port Complex, Tin Can Island, Calabar, Delta, Rivers, Onne, and Lekki Deep Sea Port indicates a signal of multi-port continuity.
- NIWA indicates a signal of inland-waterway continuity.
- NIMASA indicates a signal of maritime-safety and shipping-regulation continuity.

## Disaster-Response & Emergency Coordination Signals

- NEMA indicates a signal of national emergency-coordination continuity through a standing disaster-management institution.
- Territorial-office visibility indicates a signal of distributed emergency-presence continuity.

## Cybersecurity & Data Continuity Signals

- NITDA indicates a signal of IT-governance continuity.
- ngCERT indicates a signal of national cyber-response continuity.
- ngCERT's 24/7 monitored contact surface indicates a signal of recurring public cyber-contact continuity.
- NCCC indicates a signal of federal cybersecurity-coordination continuity where evidenced.
- NDPC indicates a signal of data-governance continuity.

## Research & Education Network Signals

- NgREN indicates a signal of national research-and-education network continuity.
- eduroam visibility indicates a signal of federation-oriented access continuity where evidenced.
- ICANN and AfriNIC responsibility references indicate a signal of externally linked research-network administrative continuity.

## Regional & International Interconnection Signals

- NiRA's `.ng` administration indicates a signal of external naming continuity.
- IXPN indicates a signal of interconnection continuity through visible exchange infrastructure.
- NgREN's ICANN and AfriNIC references indicate a signal of international administrative-interface continuity.
- FAAN's multi-airport international layer indicates a signal of recurring aviation interconnection continuity.
- NPA's multi-port environment indicates a signal of recurring maritime interconnection continuity.
- NIMASA's reference to domesticated IMO and ILO conventions indicates a signal of international standards interaction continuity where evidenced.

## Distributed Territorial Continuity Signals

- The evidence indicates a signal of Abuja-centered federal coordination paired with distributed territorial continuity.
- Lagos continuity is visible through port administration, Lagos Port Complex, Tin Can Island, Murtala Muhammed International Airport, NRC Lagos-Ibadan operations, and IXPN exchange locations.
- Distributed road, emergency, and electricity continuity is visible across the federation.
- The overall evidence supports normalization of Nigeria as a distributed state and territorial continuity environment — not Abuja-only, Lagos-only, oil-region-only, or population-defined.

## Cross-System Continuity Signals

- A recurring structural pattern is centralized federal coordination with distributed execution.
- A second recurring pattern is continuity through overlapping systems.
- A third recurring pattern is interoperability as continuity.
- Overall, the evidence supports normalization of Nigeria as an Abuja-centered federal administrative environment, a distributed territorial continuity environment, a payment-settlement interoperability environment, a telecommunications-continuity environment, an electricity-coordination environment, a maritime-support environment, a research-network-supported environment, a regional interconnection environment, and a bounded-observability environment.

## Observability Signals

- The evidence indicates incomplete telecom, private-network, cyber-operational, logistics, electricity-market, and commercial-topology visibility.
- Bounded observability therefore applies throughout.
- Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Hidden-capability inference is prohibited.

## Sources

- Derived strictly from `evidence.md` — `/atlas/jurisdiction-intelligence-engine/global/countries/nigeria/evidence.md`

# Nigeria — Evidence Layer

## Scope & Methodology

This evidence layer is derived from publicly visible sources only, principally Nigerian government portals, regulators, public operators, public institutional websites, and stable official-site search-visible records where direct extraction was limited by bot protection, dynamic rendering, DNS failures, hosting issues, or other intermittent availability. It documents observable administrative structures, infrastructure layers, continuity systems, interoperability mechanisms, and operational coordination environments visible in Nigeria.

The interpretation here is intentionally operational and infrastructure-oriented. It does not rank Nigeria, assign readiness or trust scores, infer hidden capability, infer surveillance capability, infer military or intelligence posture, create geopolitical interpretation, create West Africa or Africa leadership interpretation, create regional-power interpretation, create oil-and-gas interpretation, create population-size interpretation, create economic interpretation, or apply fintech, mobile-money, cultural-industry, gateway, or strategic-geography narratives. Public evidence is treated as bounded and incomplete by default, and the wording remains renderer-safe by limiting claims to what public sources directly expose.

## Administrative & Public-Service Infrastructure

Publicly visible state infrastructure in Nigeria presents as an Abuja-centered federal administrative environment with distributed state and sectoral continuity layers. The federal services portal publicly states that Nigeria has thirty-six states and that Abuja is the capital. The Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation publicly locates the SGF at the Shehu Shagari Complex in the Three Arms Zone, Abuja, and publicly exposes agencies directly supervised by the SGF. This supports a visible federal coordination layer concentrated in Abuja-facing institutions.

A second public-service layer is distributed across ministries, departments, agencies, and service portals rather than being confined to a single office. OSGF public materials identify directly supervised agencies including the Federal Road Safety Corps, National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure, National Boundary Commission, Bureau of Public Service Reforms, ServiCom, Fiscal Responsibility Commission, and Infrastructure Concession Regulatory Commission. Search-visible federal civil service materials also expose a ministries, departments, and agencies listing surface. Public evidence therefore supports normalization of Nigeria as an Abuja-centered federal administrative environment with distributed state and sectoral continuity, rather than as a single-node public-service stack.

## Identity & Digital-Service Infrastructure

Nigeria's publicly visible identity layer is anchored by the National Identity Management Commission. Official NIMC search-visible records present the commission as the public surface for managing the National Identification Number, enrolment, and digital identity services. Separate official NIMC records publicly describe the National Identification Number as a unique number issued after enrolment and used to match a person to biometric and other details in the National Identity Database. This is sufficient public evidence to identify a formal national identity-administration layer without inferring any non-public surveillance or verification capability.

A second visible layer exists through federal digital-service access surfaces. The federal services portal publicly presents Nigeria's government-services gateway and exposes NIMC as a service provider with public pages for NIN pre-enrolment and self-service modification workflows. Public evidence therefore supports normalization of Nigeria as an identity-and-service environment with national enrolment, NIN issuance, identity-data update surfaces, and federal online service access, while deeper backend identity-validation architecture remains only partly visible.

## Payment & Financial Infrastructure

Nigeria's publicly visible payment infrastructure is organized around the Central Bank of Nigeria and the national payments system. CBN publicly states that its payments-system supervision mandate is to ensure the soundness and safety of the payments system through rules and guidelines. Official CBN search-visible materials identify banks, discount houses, the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System, the Nigeria Stock Exchange, payment service providers, and switching companies as key players in the Nigerian payments system under central oversight. CBN public materials also expose standing national payment initiatives including NUBAN, cheque truncation, the National Central Switch, the Nigeria Electronic Fraud Forum, and RTGS deployment.

The large-value settlement layer is clearly visible through CBN's RTGS and Scripless Securities Settlement System. CBN publicly states that RTGS operations commenced in December 2006, that a replacement RTGS system and central securities depository were deployed in December 2013, and that the RTGS and S4 environment was upgraded in April 2023 with ISO 20022 support, API integration with other financial market infrastructures, and four settlement sessions. CBN's public payment-modes materials also identify NEFT and NIBSS Instant Payment within the non-cash payment environment.

Retail and interbank interoperability are additionally visible through NIBSS and the CBN licensing structure. Official NIBSS search-visible records describe NIBSS as an inter-bank settlement system serving licensed banks, describe NIBSS Instant Payment as a deferred net settlement system in which funds become available in the beneficiary account in real time before settlement, and expose the Nigeria Central Switch as a public switching and interconnectivity layer. CBN's public payment-service-provider directory further exposes licensed card schemes, switching and processing licensees, mobile-money operator licensees, and payment solution service providers. Public evidence therefore supports normalization of Nigeria as a payment-settlement interoperability environment with central-bank oversight, visible interbank rails, switching infrastructure, and licensed provider layers.

## Telecommunications & Connectivity Infrastructure

Telecommunications in Nigeria are publicly visible as a regulated communications environment. The Nigerian Communications Commission publicly describes itself as responsible for creating an enabling environment for competition among operators and for ensuring provision of qualitative and efficient telecommunications services throughout the country.

A second visible layer is country-domain administration and internet-exchange infrastructure. NiRA publicly states that it is the registry for the .ng country-code top-level domain, that it maintains the registry database for registered .ng names, and that it operates a registry-registrar-registrant model rather than direct end-user registration. Official IXPN search-visible records describe the Internet Exchange Point of Nigeria as a neutral, membership-based, not-for-profit organization, while IXPN traffic-statistics surfaces publicly expose exchange activity across multiple Lagos exchange locations.

## Electricity & Energy Infrastructure

Nigeria's publicly visible electricity environment is organized around transmission, regulation, and market-pool coordination. The Transmission Company of Nigeria publicly presents itself as a transmission and system-operations company based in Abuja and explicitly distinguishes itself from distribution companies that supply electricity directly to homes. Search-visible NERC materials publicly state that the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission was established by the Electricity Act 2023 as an independent regulatory body with the mandate to regulate the Nigerian Electricity Supply Industry.

A second visible layer exists through market-pool administration. NBET publicly states that the Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc is the manager and administrator of the electricity pool in the Nigerian electricity supply industry and that it is wholly owned by the Federal Government of Nigeria.

## Transportation Infrastructure

Nigeria's publicly visible transport environment is organized through a national ministry layer and separate road and rail continuity layers. The Federal Ministry of Transportation publicly exposes departments for rail transport services, road transport and mass transit administration, maritime services, and transport planning and coordination.

Road continuity is also visible through the Federal Ministry of Works and the Federal Roads Maintenance Agency. FERMA search-visible materials describe the agency as Nigeria's institutional mechanism for monitoring and maintaining federal roads.

Rail continuity is publicly visible through the Nigerian Railway Corporation. NRC publicly presents the railway system as the oldest modern form of transportation in Nigeria, describes a 1067 mm Cape-gauge track system, and exposes passenger, excursion, and freight services together with current operational notices, including Lagos-Ibadan service updates.

## Aviation Infrastructure

Nigeria's aviation infrastructure is publicly visible through the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority, the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria, and the Nigerian Airspace Management Agency. NCAA public materials describe the authority as responsible for aviation safety and economic regulation.

Airport continuity is visibly organized through FAAN. FAAN publicly states that it manages all commercial airports in Nigeria and identifies Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos, Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja, Mallam Aminu Kano International Airport, Port Harcourt International Airport, and Akanu Ibiam International Airport in Enugu.

Air-navigation continuity is publicly visible through NAMA. NAMA publicly states that it was established by Act No. 48 of 1999 and describes it as the air navigation service provider responsible for managing Nigerian airspace in line with ICAO standards and recommended practices.

## Maritime & Port Infrastructure

Nigeria's maritime and port environment is publicly visible through the Nigerian Ports Authority. NPA publicly states that it is the federal government agency that governs and operates ports in Nigeria and identifies major ports including Lagos Port Complex, Tin Can Island Port Complex, Calabar Port Complex, Delta Ports, Rivers Port Complex, Onne Port Complex, and Lekki Deep Sea Port.

A second visible layer exists through inland waterways administration. NIWA publicly states that it was established under the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria and was given primary responsibility to improve and develop Nigeria's inland waterways for navigation.

A third visible layer is maritime safety and regulatory administration. NIMASA publicly states that it was established for maritime safety, seafarers standards, maritime labour, shipping regulation, cabotage administration, pollution prevention and control, port and flag state duties, and implementation of domesticated IMO and ILO conventions.

## Disaster-Response & Emergency Coordination Infrastructure

Nigeria's public emergency-coordination layer is visible through the National Emergency Management Agency. Official NEMA search-visible records state that the agency was established to manage disasters in Nigeria and describe its mission as coordinating resources for disaster prevention, preparedness, mitigation, and response.

Public NEMA materials also show ongoing operational coordination including fire-risk cautions, climate-risk early-warning activity, multi-agency response to a market fire in Kano, and post-flood assessment activity in Lagos.

## Cybersecurity & Data Infrastructure

Nigeria's publicly visible cyber-governance layer includes NITDA, ngCERT, the National Cybersecurity Coordination Centre, and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission. Official NITDA search-visible materials describe the agency's mandate as operating and implementing national IT policy and creating a framework for planning, research, development, standardization, application, coordination, monitoring, evaluation, and regulation of information-technology practices in Nigeria.

Public cyber-incident coordination is also visible. Official ngCERT search-visible materials describe the Nigeria Computer Emergency Response Team as established to manage cyber-threat risks in Nigeria's cyberspace and to coordinate incident response and mitigation strategies. Public ngCERT RFC2350 records additionally expose a 24/7 monitored operational contact surface.

A data-governance layer is publicly visible through the Nigeria Data Protection Commission. Official NDPC search-visible materials describe the commission as Nigeria's data protection authority under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.

## Research & Education Network Infrastructure

Nigeria's research and education network layer is publicly visible through NgREN. NgREN publicly states that it was incorporated as a private company limited by guarantee on 21 February 2012 and that it provides connectivity infrastructure for service delivery to its members. NgREN also publicly states that it assumes legal and technical responsibilities to ICANN and AfriNIC while operating within Nigerian corporate law.

A second visible layer exists through institutional services and federation-oriented connectivity. NgREN publicly exposes high-speed internet connectivity, capacity-building services, eduroam, the NIRIS project, and high-performance computing support.

## Regional & International Connectivity Infrastructure

Nigeria's regional and international connectivity is publicly visible across domain administration, internet exchange, research networking, aviation, and maritime administration. NiRA administers the .ng country-code domain environment, while IXPN publicly exposes interconnection infrastructure and traffic-statistics surfaces. NgREN publicly states that it operates with ICANN and AfriNIC responsibilities and exposes eduroam service.

International transport continuity is also directly visible. FAAN publicly identifies a multi-airport international aviation layer spanning Abuja, Lagos, Kano, Port Harcourt, and Enugu. NPA publicly identifies a multi-port seaport environment spanning Lagos, Tin Can, Calabar, Delta, Rivers, and Onne, while NIMASA publicly identifies implementation of domesticated IMO and ILO conventions.

## Distributed Territorial Continuity Infrastructure

Public evidence supports normalization of Nigeria as both an Abuja-centered and territorially distributed continuity environment. Administrative concentration is visible through Abuja's status as the federal capital and through Abuja-facing institutional surfaces including the OSGF, the federal services portal, TCN, NERC-related public materials, FAAN headquarters, and other federal regulators and agencies.

At the same time, critical continuity is not confined to Abuja. Lagos continuity is publicly visible through the NPA head office, Lagos Port Complex, Tin Can Island Port Complex, Murtala Muhammed International Airport, NRC Lagos-Ibadan operations, and IXPN's publicly visible Lagos exchange locations. Additional territorial continuity is visible through Port Harcourt and Onne maritime infrastructure in Rivers State, international airport nodes in Kano, Port Harcourt, and Enugu, FERMA's road-maintenance structure, and NEMA's incident activity across multiple states.

## Structural Constraints & Evidence Boundaries

This file is public-source-bound. Telecom visibility is incomplete, especially for private backbone routes, full carrier interconnection maps, enterprise connectivity, and deeper commercial operator topology. Private-network visibility is incomplete across banking, telecommunications, enterprise, port, airport, and government-contractor environments. Cyber-operational visibility is incomplete beyond the public existence of NITDA, ngCERT, NCCC, NDPC, and their published mandates or public-facing coordination surfaces. Logistics visibility is incomplete for private freight routing, warehousing, inland-distribution practice, and non-public contingency procedures. Commercial-topology visibility is incomplete for bank-to-bank dependencies beyond published rails, private telecom peering, terminal operating arrangements, and backend service-provider dependencies. Electricity-market visibility is incomplete for full dispatch logic, balancing practice, and detailed contractual structure beyond publicly identified institutions.

Bounded observability therefore applies throughout. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Hidden-capability inference is prohibited.

## Sources

- Federal services portal: https://services.gov.ng/
- Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation: https://www.osgf.gov.ng/
- OSGF agencies page: https://www.osgf.gov.ng/about/agencies/
- Federation Civil Service Commission MDA listing surface: https://fedcivilservice.gov.ng/mdas
- National Identity Management Commission: https://nimc.gov.ng/
- NIMC NIN page: https://nimc.gov.ng/nin

# Nigeria — Change Log

## Change-Log Scope

- This file is the final derivative layer for Nigeria and derives strictly from `evidence.md`, `signals.md`, `trust-dimensions.md`, `metadata.md`, `profile.md`, and `builder-mode.md`.
- It documents normalization convergence, recurring structural characteristics, recurring interaction characteristics, structural exclusions, bounded observability, and canonical Atlas identity only.
- No rankings, scores, trust levels, readiness levels, certifications, deployment meanings, deployment guidance, or Atlas surface assignments exist in this file.
- No geopolitical meaning, West Africa leadership meaning, Africa-leadership meaning, regional-power meaning, oil-and-gas meaning, population-scale meaning, economic-power meaning, fintech meaning, mobile-money meaning, gateway meaning, or strategic-geography meaning exists in this file.
- All statements remain evidence-bound, renderer-safe, and bounded by incomplete public observability.

## Normalization Summary

- Nigeria normalized as an Abuja-centered federal coordination environment with Lagos-linked operational reinforcement rather than a single-node national operating model.
- It normalized as a distributed state and territorial continuity environment rather than an Abuja-only or Lagos-only structure.
- It normalized as a payment-settlement interoperability environment through Central Bank of Nigeria continuity, National Payments System continuity, Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System continuity, RTGS and S4 continuity, NIBSS Instant Payment continuity, Nigeria Central Switch continuity, and licensed-provider interaction rather than a fragmented payment model.
- It normalized as a telecom-domain-exchange continuity environment through Nigerian Communications Commission continuity, `.ng` continuity, Nigeria Internet Registration Association continuity, and Internet Exchange Point of Nigeria continuity rather than a purely operator-defined communications environment.
- It normalized as an electricity coordination environment through Transmission Company of Nigeria continuity, Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission continuity, Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc continuity, transmission continuity, and system-operation continuity rather than a detached electricity model.
- It normalized as a maritime-support continuity environment through Nigerian Ports Authority continuity, National Inland Waterways Authority continuity, Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency continuity, and visible multi-port continuity rather than a gateway-framed maritime model.
- It normalized as a research-network-supported continuity environment through Nigerian Research and Education Network continuity, academic-network continuity, institutional-connectivity continuity, eduroam continuity where evidenced, and research-service continuity rather than a commercial-connectivity-only environment.
- It normalized as a regional interconnection environment through naming governance, exchange continuity, aviation interfaces, maritime interfaces, research-network external relationships, and standards interaction where evidenced rather than geopolitical framing.
- It normalized as a bounded-observability environment in which continuity is visible across multiple public layers while deeper private, cyber-operational, logistics, electricity-market, and commercial topology remains only partly visible.
- Nigeria did not normalize as Abuja-only, Lagos-only, oil-defined, population-defined, regional-power-defined, or fintech-defined.

## Recurring Administrative Characteristics

- Abuja-centered federal coordination remained the strongest recurring administrative characteristic across the package.
- OSGF continuity remained recurring through visible federal coordination and supervised-agency interaction rather than capital-only symbolic presence.
- Ministry, department, and agency interaction remained recurring through multi-agency public-service continuity rather than a single consolidated administrative stack.
- Regulator-service interaction remained recurring through the coexistence of federal institutions, sector regulators, and service-access layers rather than one-body institutional control.
- State-level distribution remained recurring through the thirty-six-state environment and distributed sectoral continuity rather than a capital-confined administrative model.
- Centralized coordination with distributed execution remained the dominant administrative pattern.
- Administrative normalization remained descriptive only and did not produce political interpretation, governance scoring, or state-capacity claims.

## Recurring Payment & Financial Characteristics

- Central Bank of Nigeria continuity remained the principal recurring payment characteristic through visible coordination, supervision, rules, settlement, and participant oversight.
- National Payments System continuity remained recurring through a multi-participant environment rather than a single settlement rail.
- Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System continuity remained recurring through interbank interoperability rather than bank-by-bank isolated transfer handling.
- RTGS and S4 continuity remained recurring through large-value settlement visibility inside the wider payment environment rather than retail-only payment visibility.
- NIBSS Instant Payment continuity remained recurring through instant-payment handling within the wider settlement environment rather than detached transfer pathways.
- Nigeria Central Switch continuity remained recurring through visible switching and interconnectivity interaction rather than payment-routing silos.
- Licensed-provider interaction remained recurring across switching, processing, card-scheme, and payment-service layers rather than a closed bank-only arrangement.
- Settlement interoperability remained the dominant recurring payment pattern.
- Final characterization: payment-settlement interoperability continuity.

## Recurring Telecommunications Characteristics

- Nigerian Communications Commission continuity remained the clearest recurring regulatory characteristic across the communications environment.
- `.ng` continuity remained visible through formal country-domain administration rather than unmanaged namespace dependence.
- Nigeria Internet Registration Association continuity remained recurring as the naming-governance layer for `.ng`.
- Internet Exchange Point of Nigeria continuity remained recurring through visible exchange and interconnection activity.
- Telecom-domain-exchange continuity remained the dominant communications characterization.

## Recurring Electricity Characteristics

- Transmission Company of Nigeria continuity remained the principal electricity-coordination characteristic.
- Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission continuity remained recurring through standing electricity-regulatory visibility.
- Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc continuity remained recurring through pool-administration visibility.
- Final characterization: electricity-regulator-transmission continuity.

## Recurring Transportation Characteristics

- Federal transport coordination remained the strongest recurring transport characteristic.
- FERMA continuity remained recurring through road-maintenance and road-support visibility.
- Nigerian Railway Corporation continuity remained recurring through passenger, excursion, freight, and route-service visibility.
- Transportation normalization remained operational only.

## Recurring Aviation Characteristics

- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority continuity remained the clearest recurring aviation-oversight characteristic.
- Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria continuity remained recurring through visible multi-airport administration.
- Nigerian Airspace Management Agency continuity remained recurring through air-navigation and airspace-management visibility.
- Distributed airport continuity remained recurring through Abuja, Lagos, Kano, Port Harcourt, and Enugu.

## Recurring Maritime Characteristics

- Nigerian Ports Authority continuity remained the principal maritime administrative characteristic.
- Lagos Port Complex, Tin Can Island, and Onne continuity remained recurring as visible port nodes.
- National Inland Waterways Authority continuity remained recurring through inland-waterway interaction.
- Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency continuity remained recurring through maritime-safety and shipping-regulation visibility.
- Final characterization: maritime-support continuity.

## Recurring Emergency Coordination Characteristics

- National Emergency Management Agency continuity remained the clearest recurring emergency-coordination characteristic.
- Preparedness continuity remained recurring through public warning, assessment, and prevention-related surfaces.
- Territorial emergency distribution remained recurring through territorial-office visibility.

## Recurring Cybersecurity & Data Characteristics

- National Information Technology Development Agency continuity remained the clearest recurring IT-governance characteristic.
- ngCERT continuity remained recurring through named cyber-response coordination.
- NCCC continuity where evidenced remained recurring through federal cybersecurity-coordination visibility.
- Nigeria Data Protection Commission continuity remained recurring through data-governance visibility.
- Final characterization: cyber-data-governance interaction continuity.

## Recurring Research & Education Network Characteristics

- Nigerian Research and Education Network continuity remained the clearest recurring research-network characteristic.
- eduroam continuity remained recurring where evidenced.
- Final characterization: research-network-supported continuity.

## Structural Exclusions

- Nigeria was not normalized as a geopolitical power.
- Nigeria was not normalized as a West Africa leader.
- Nigeria was not normalized as an Africa leader.
- Nigeria was not normalized as a regional power.
- Nigeria was not normalized as an oil economy.
- Nigeria was not normalized as a population-scale environment.
- Nigeria was not normalized as an economic power.
- Nigeria was not normalized as a fintech environment.
- Nigeria was not normalized as a mobile-money environment.
- Nigeria was not normalized as a cultural influence environment.
- Nigeria was not normalized as a security/conflict environment.
- Nigeria was not normalized as a gateway-to-Africa environment.
- Nigeria was not normalized as a strategic geography environment.

## Bounded Observability Record

- Bounded observability remained a standing package characteristic throughout normalization.
- Incomplete telecom visibility remained explicit for private backbone routes, full carrier interconnection maps, enterprise connectivity, and deeper commercial operator topology.
- Incomplete private-network visibility remained explicit across banking, telecommunications, enterprise, port, airport, and government-contractor environments.
- Incomplete cyber-operational visibility remained explicit beyond the public existence of NITDA, ngCERT, NCCC, NDPC, and their visible coordination or compliance surfaces.
- Incomplete logistics visibility remained explicit for private freight routing, warehousing, inland-distribution practice, and non-public contingency procedures.
- Incomplete electricity-market visibility remained explicit for dispatch logic, balancing practice, and detailed contractual structure beyond publicly identified institutions.
- Incomplete commercial-topology visibility remained explicit for bank-to-bank dependencies beyond published rails, private telecom peering, terminal operating arrangements, and backend service-provider dependencies.
- Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
- Hidden-capability inference is prohibited.

## Canonical Normalization Result

- Nigeria normalized as an Abuja-centered federal coordination environment with Lagos-linked operational reinforcement, distributed multi-node territorial continuity, payment-settlement interoperability, telecom-domain-exchange continuity, electricity coordination, maritime support, research-network-supported continuity, regional interconnection, and bounded observability.
- Centralized coordination with distributed execution remained the dominant recurring structural pattern.
- Continuity-through-overlapping systems remained the dominant recurring continuity pattern.
- Interoperability as continuity remained the dominant recurring interoperability pattern.
- The completed package remained infrastructure-first, operational, non-ranking, non-geopolitical, and bounded by incomplete public observability.
- Normalization status: complete.
